entities.summary:
Borobudur is the world's largest Buddhist temple, a 9th-century Mahayana Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia. Built around 800 CE during the Sailendra dynasty's rule, it consists of nine stacked platforms of diminishing size crowned by a central dome, decorated with 2,672 relief panels and 504 Buddha statues — creating the world's largest and most complete ensemble of Buddhist bas-reliefs.

Borobudur's design represents the Buddhist cosmological universe: the three lowest levels (Kamadhatu) represent the world of desire; the five square platforms (Rupadhatu) represent the world of forms; and the three circular platforms (Arupadhatu) represent the formless world. Pilgrims travel the 5-kilometer path ascending through these levels in a ritual representing the journey from ignorance to enlightenment. The 72 perforated bell-shaped stupas on the upper terraces each contain a Buddha statue.

Abandoned around 1000 CE due to volcanic eruptions and population shifts, Borobudur was buried under volcanic ash and jungle until 1814, when colonial official Herman Cornelius Hartmann and later British Governor Thomas Stamford Raffles organized excavation. The UNESCO-funded restoration of 1973-1983, costing $25 million, cleaned and stabilized the 2 million stone blocks. Today Borobudur receives 5 million visitors annually and hosts the Vesak Day celebration attended by thousands of Buddhists.
